Conversely, systematically suppressing your emotions costs energy and does not reduce what you feel. The emotion is not the enemy; what matters is what you do with it.

Restating what the other person said, "if I understand correctly, you…", shows you have understood and lets them correct you. He learned lists of meaningless syllables, like "DAX" or "BOK", so that nothing would latch onto an existing memory, then measured what remained. In 1885 he published Über das Gedächtnis: we forget very fast at first, especially in the first hours, then more and more slowly.

The shocks were fake, the learner an actor who screamed. Under the calm pressure of an experimenter in a lab coat, 65 % of participants in the main version went up to the maximum 450-volt shock.

The Stanford prison experiment, run by Philip Zimbardo in 1971, is now heavily disputed: archives show the "guards" were encouraged to be harsh. And the story of Kitty Genovese, killed in 1964 in front of "38 witnesses" who did nothing, was exaggerated: there were far fewer, and the police were called.

In 1969 Bibb Latané and Judith Rodin had people hear a woman fall in the next room: 70 % of those alone went to help, against 40 % when paired with a stranger.
En groupe, les opinions se durcissent au: In groups, opinions also harden: group polarisation pushes towards the already dominant position. And groupthink can lead experts to bad collective decisions: Irving Janis illustrated it in 1972 with the failed Bay of Pigs landing. Antidote: appoint a devil's advocate, and ask for opinions before the leader gives theirs.

Some functions are more lateralised, like language, but the two hemispheres work together constantly. In 2013 a study of more than 1,000 brains by Jared Nielsen and colleagues found no overall "dominance" of one hemisphere in individuals.

A pretty coloured image is not proof. And the brain feels no pain: some operations are done on an awake patient, who talks during the procedure.

That is theory of mind, tested this way by Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith in 1985.

You mentally place each item to remember in a familiar place, then walk the route again to find them. Antithesis: an opposite state produces the opposite gesture. And the direct action of the nervous system, which acts on the body independently of the will. Conclusion: the great expressions are shared, inherited from common ancestors.
Un siècle plus tard, Paul Ekman et Walla: A century later, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen showed that Fore people of Papua New Guinea, without writing, recognised the same expressions. In 1978, they completed a coding system for facial movements, in which each movement is an "action unit". Ekman would advise the series Lie to Me and Pixar's film Inside Out, in 2015. But the universality of emotions is still debated.

With the two points of a compass placed on the skin, he sought the distance at which one feels two points instead of one. With weights, he showed that one best distinguishes two masses that differ by 8 to 10%: for a 100 g block, one needs at least 108 g.

Gustav Fechner, who had damaged his eyes in 1839 by looking at the Sun, drew a law from it: for sensation to rise steadily, the stimulus must increase in geometric progression. In 1860 he published his Elements of Psychophysics: psychology had its first equations.

Wilhelm Wundt naît en 1832 près de Mannh: Wilhelm Wundt was born in 1832 near Mannheim. In 1858, he became assistant to the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz at Heidelberg. In 1874, he published the Principles of Physiological Psychology, the first textbook of experimental psychology. Appointed professor of philosophy at Leipzig in 1875, he opened there in 1879 the first laboratory devoted entirely to psychology.
Il y dirige 185 thèses entre 1875 et 191: There he supervised 185 theses between 1875 and 1919, 70 of them by foreign students; among them were James McKeen Cattell, Granville Stanley Hall, Edward Titchener and Hugo Münsterberg. Wundt rejected naive introspection: self-observation has to be learned. He described feelings along three dimensions: pleasant or unpleasant, tense or relaxed, excited or calm.

Dès 1865, l'ophtalmologiste néerlandais: From 1865, the Dutch ophthalmologist Franciscus Donders measured reaction times. A subject repeats a syllable known in advance (method a), or one of five possible syllables (method b), or only one particular syllable among five (method c). In 1868, he found that c takes 0.047 s longer than a: the time to discriminate; and b, 0.036 s longer than c: the time to choose.
C'est la méthode de soustraction : retra: This is the subtraction method: subtracting a simple time from a more complex one to measure a step of thought. A simple reaction time is around 200 ms; in young adults, about 160 ms for a sound and 190 ms for a light. Francis Galton would measure more than 10,000 among the London public. In Leipzig, Wundt made such timings a routine.
Donders (1868) : discriminer, 47 ms ; ch: Donders (1868): discriminating, 47 ms; choosing, 36 ms. Reacting to a sound, about 160 ms; to a light, about 190 ms.

Ivan Pavlov naît en 1849 à Riazan, fils: Ivan Pavlov was born in 1849 in Ryazan, the son of a village Orthodox priest; he left the seminary without graduating to devote himself to science. A physiologist, he fitted his dogs with fistulas to collect their digestive juices over long periods. In 1904, he received the Nobel Prize for his work on digestion: the first Russian Nobel laureate.
Il remarque que ses chiens salivent avan: He noticed that his dogs salivated before the food arrived: he called it "psychic secretion". He then paired a stimulus, such as a metronome, with the meal; soon the metronome alone made them salivate. He published these results in 1897. And the bell? His writings mention metronomes, whistles, tuning forks and electric shocks; whether he ever used a bell is still disputed.
Nobel 1904 pour la digestion ; la « sécr: Nobel 1904 for digestion; "psychic secretion"; a metronome, more surely than a bell.
Le vocabulaire est resté. La nourriture: The vocabulary has stayed. Food is an unconditioned stimulus: it makes the dog salivate without learning, which is the unconditioned response. The metronome, at first neutral, becomes a conditioned stimulus after announcing food; the salivation it triggers on its own is the conditioned response, learned and less lasting than the innate reflex.
Si le métronome sonne sans nourriture, l: If the metronome sounds without food, the response eventually dies out: this is extinction, which does not erase the learning, for after a rest the response can return, weaker. A similar sound also triggers the response: this is generalisation. Conscious to the end, Pavlov had a student sit by his deathbed, in 1936, to note what he felt as he died.
Stimulus et réponse inconditionnels, pui: Unconditioned stimulus and response, then conditioned ones; extinction, recovery, generalisation.

Watson published his manifesto, "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It": psychology must be a purely objective experimental branch of natural science. In 1920, with his student Rosalie Rayner, he conditioned a nine-month-old baby, "Albert": each time the child touched a white rat, a steel bar was struck with a hammer behind his back.
Bientôt le rat seul fait pleurer Albert,: Soon the rat alone made Albert cry, then a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat, a Santa Claus mask with a cotton beard. Such an experiment would be considered unethical today. Before them, Edward Thorndike had proposed the law of effect in 1898; B. F. Skinner would extend it with his lever box, which he hated hearing called a "Skinner box".
Watson (1913) : n'étudier que le comport: Watson (1913): study behaviour alone. Little Albert (1920): a learned fear, then generalised.
À Vienne, autour de 1900, Freud fait par: In Vienna, around 1900, Freud got his patients talking and read their dreams: psychoanalysis looked for what escapes consciousness.

Avec Josef Breuer, Freud publie en 1895: With Josef Breuer, Freud published Studies on Hysteria in 1895; the patient "Anna O." spoke of a "talking cure".
L'Interprétation des rêves paraît le 4 n: The Interpretation of Dreams appeared on 4 November 1899, dated 1900: every dream fulfils a wish.

La psychanalyse a marqué la culture du X: Psychoanalysis left its mark on 20th-century culture, but its effectiveness and scientific status remain much debated.
Sigmund Freud naît le 6 mai 1856 à Freib: Sigmund Freud was born on 6 May 1856 at Freiberg, in Moravia, now Příbor in Czechia. A young Viennese neurologist, he praised the virtues of cocaine in 1884 in "On Coca", before ceasing to recommend it in the face of cases of addiction. In October 1885, he went to Paris for three months to study with Charcot, who was working on hypnosis.
Son aîné Josef Breuer soigne Bertha Papp: His elder Josef Breuer treated Bertha Pappenheim, "Anna O.", who coined the phrase "talking cure". In 1895, Freud and Breuer published Studies on Hysteria. Freud then abandoned hypnosis for free association: the patient says whatever comes to mind. He named his method "psychoanalysis" in 1896. The patient lies on a couch, the analyst sits behind, out of sight.
Charcot (1885), Anna O. et la « cure par: Charcot (1885), Anna O. and the "talking cure", free association; the word "psychoanalysis" in 1896.
L'Interprétation des rêves paraît le 4 n: The Interpretation of Dreams appeared on 4 November 1899 from Franz Deuticke, dated 1900. Thesis: every dream is the fulfilment of a wish. The manifest content, the one we remember, disguises a latent content; during sleep, the unconscious condenses and displaces images, so that on waking the meaning is unrecognisable.
« L'interprétation des rêves est la voie: "The interpretation of dreams is the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind," wrote Freud. His first example is one of his own dreams, that of "Irma's injection", from the summer of 1895. Success was slow: the first printing, 600 copies, took eight years to sell. In 1901, The Psychopathology of Everyday Life tracked the unconscious in slips and forgettings.
1899 : le rêve accomplit un désir déguis: 1899: the dream fulfils a disguised wish; 600 copies, eight years to sell them.
Le ça, le moi, le surmoi: The id, the ego, the superego
En 1923, dans Le Moi et le Ça, Freud déc: In 1923, in The Ego and the Id, Freud described three agencies. The id, present from birth, a reservoir of drives, unconscious, obeys the pleasure principle. The ego forms slowly and negotiates between drives and reality, according to the reality principle. The superego is the part of the ego where self-observation, self-criticism and judgement arise.

He died in London on 23 September 1939. The philosopher Karl Popper would criticise psychoanalysis as unfalsifiable: a theory that explains everything cannot be proved wrong, and so is not scientific.
Ça, moi, surmoi (1923) ; les livres brûl: Id, ego, superego (1923); the books burned in 1933; Popper: an unfalsifiable theory is not science.

En 1904, une commission du ministère cha: In 1904, a ministry commission tasked Alfred Binet with spotting pupils who needed adapted teaching.
En 1905, Binet et Théodore Simon publien: In 1905, Binet and Théodore Simon published a scale of thirty tasks; in 1908 came mental age.

Alfred Binet naît à Nice le 8 juillet 18: Alfred Binet was born in Nice on 8 July 1857. With a law degree in 1878, he turned to psychology and worked at the Salpêtrière with Charcot. He also observed his two daughters very closely. In 1891, he joined the psychology laboratory at the Sorbonne, which he directed from 1894 or 1895 depending on the sources.
En 1894, il fonde avec Henry Beaunis la: In 1894, he founded with Henry Beaunis the journal L'Année psychologique. The same year, he published a Psychology of Great Calculators and Chess Players. In 1904, the Ministry of Public Instruction set up a commission for struggling pupils; Binet was on it. He needed a tool to recognise those who needed help.
Binet, de la Salpêtrière à la Sorbonne ;: Binet, from the Salpêtrière to the Sorbonne; 1904, a commission and a need: to spot the pupils who need help.
Trente épreuves et un âge mental: Thirty tasks and a mental age
En 1905, Binet et Théodore Simon publien: In 1905, Binet and Théodore Simon published their scale: thirty tasks of increasing difficulty, from grasping an object or recognising food to repeating digits, comparing lines of different lengths or answering an abstract question. The test takes about a quarter of an hour.
La version de 1908 range les épreuves pa: The 1908 version arranged the tasks by age: the birth of mental age, the age whose tasks a child succeeds at. In 1911, Binet revised the test without Simon, with five tasks per age, and died the same year. For him as for Simon, intelligence is malleable: the test is there to help, not to condemn.
1905, trente épreuves ; 1908, l'âge ment: 1905, thirty tasks; 1908, mental age; a malleable intelligence, to be helped.
En 1912, l'Allemand William Stern propos: In 1912, the German William Stern proposed dividing mental age by real age and multiplying by 100: the Intelligenzquotient, the IQ. Simon saw it as a betrayal of the test's purpose. In 1916, Lewis Terman, at Stanford, revised the scale and made it the most used test in the United States for decades. During the First World War, 1.75 million American soldiers took written tests.
Les tests modernes ne calculent plus un: Modern tests no longer compute a quotient: they place each person on a curve with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, where about two people in three are between 85 and 115. And raw scores rise by about three points per decade: the Flynn effect. In 1981, Stephen Jay Gould denounced in The Mismeasure of Man the idea of summing up intelligence in a single number.
Stern (1912) : QI = âge mental ÷ âge rée: Stern (1912): IQ = mental age ÷ real age × 100. Today: mean 100, standard deviation 15; Flynn effect.
Le stress de Selye, l'adaptation hédoniq: Selye's stress, hedonic adaptation, sleep, and Csíkszentmihályi's flow: what wears us down and what makes us happy.

A loved one's pain: the anterior insula and cingulate become active, not the areas that locate pain (Singer, 2004). The role of mirror neurons in empathy is still debated.
Une piste célèbre vient du singe. Dans l: A famous lead comes from the monkey. In the 1980s and 1990s, at the University of Parma, Giacomo Rizzolatti and his colleagues placed electrodes in a motor area of the macaque brain. Some neurons fired when the monkey grasped food, but also when it watched a human grasp it. They were called mirror neurons: as if the brain silently replayed the other's gesture.
En 2004, Tania Singer et ses collègues,: In 2004, Tania Singer and her colleagues, in London, studied 16 couples. In the scanner, the woman received a painful stimulus on her hand, or saw a signal showing that her partner, next to her, was receiving it. In both cases, two regions became active: the anterior insula and the anterior cingulate cortex, linked to the emotional, unpleasant side of pain. The areas that say where it hurts and how much responded only to her own pain. We feel the other's “it hurts”, not their hand.
Prudence pourtant. Chez l'humain, on peu: Caution, though. In humans, a single neuron can rarely be recorded: in 2010, Roy Mukamel's team managed it in patients treated for epilepsy, and found a few neurons active both for an action performed and for an action observed. In 2009, the neuroscientist Gregory Hickok objected that the idea that they serve to understand actions had never really been tested, even in monkeys. The role of mirror neurons in empathy is not settled; the shared pain regions, too, remain a hypothesis based on a small number of people.
Comment un neurone passe un message: How a neuron passes on a message
L'influx nerveux : une inversion de char: The nerve impulse: a reversal of charge lasting about a thousandth of a second that runs along the axon, all or nothing. At the synapse, it releases neurotransmitters that cross the cleft. Loewi (1921): two frog hearts and a fluid that slows them down.
Un neurone reçoit des messages par ses d: A neuron receives messages through its dendrites, thin branches, and sends them along a long wire, the axon. At rest, the inside of the cell is negatively charged, about −70 millivolts. When it receives enough signals, sodium ions rush in and reverse the charge: this is the nerve impulse, or action potential. The whole thing lasts about a thousandth of a second, and the wave runs along the axon like a flame along a fuse, at 1 to over 100 metres per second.
C'est tout ou rien : un influx ne part p: It is all or nothing: an impulse does not fire “a little”. To say “strong”, the neuron does not shout louder, it sends more impulses per second. At the end of the axon, it does not touch the next neuron: a tiny space separates them, the synaptic cleft. There the impulse releases molecules, neurotransmitters, which cross the cleft and stimulate or slow down the cell opposite.
Que le message traverse la fente grâce à: It was Otto Loewi who showed that the message crosses the cleft through a chemical. On the night of Easter Saturday 1921, he dreamed of an experiment and jotted it down, but could not read his notes in the morning; the next night, he had the same dream and rushed to the laboratory. He stimulated the vagus nerve of a frog heart, which slowed down, then poured the fluid that bathed it onto a second heart: it slowed down too. The nerve had released a substance, later identified as acetylcholine. Loewi shared the 1936 Nobel Prize with Henry Dale.
Deux vitesses : les nerfs et l'adrénalin: Two speeds: nerves and adrenaline first (fight or flight, Cannon, 1914), then the relay of hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenals and their cortisol. Cortisol slows its own production. Chronic stress: the loop no longer switches off.
Face à un danger, le corps a deux vitess: Faced with danger, the body has two speeds. The first goes through the nerves: the amygdala, a small structure in the brain, alerts the hypothalamus, and the nerves of the sympathetic system make the core of the adrenal glands release adrenaline. The heart beats faster, breathing quickens, the liver releases sugar into the blood, the pupils widen, digestion slows down. The American physiologist Walter Cannon described this fight-or-flight response in 1914.
La seconde vitesse passe par les hormone: The second speed goes through hormones, in relay. The hypothalamus releases a hormone, CRH, which pushes the pituitary gland to release ACTH, which orders the outer layer of the adrenal glands to produce cortisol. Cortisol raises blood pressure and available sugar, and puts the immune system on hold: useful to sustain an effort. Then it slows down the production of CRH and ACTH itself, like a thermostat switching off the heating: the loop closes.
Le problème vient quand la boucle ne se: The trouble starts when the loop no longer switches off. Prolonged exposure to high levels of cortisol is believed to shrink the hippocampus, which serves memory, in severely stressed people and animals; an abnormally flattened cortisol cycle is linked to insomnia and burnout. That is the whole difference between acute stress, which helps us cope, and chronic stress, which wears us down.
